Q: Apply aero glass blur to a specific control area in WPF A:

Unfortunately, there is no method by which you can enable a blur-behind effect on a standard WPF control. However, some controls (popups, menus, and other windows) are technically rendered inside other windows. You can retrieve the Handle to the underlying window and pass that to a DWM function. Another tricky method is to host native controls in a HwndHost. However, this causes its own issues. HwndHost only supports native content, meaning you can’t just drop a WPF control inside. Your best option for blurring a specific portion of your window is to create a new window, set the start position to manual, set top and left to specific points relative to the main window, and set up logic such that the new window moves and resizes with the main window. All you’d have to do then is apply whatever DWM or composition effect you want on the new window. This usually isn’t practical, especially if you want that piece of your main window to be constantly blurred, and even more so if your app can be dragged and resized.

Q: Why is rep movsb slow for overlapping forward memmove, and why does libc use it? A:

In the quoted case, there are two independent thresholds:

  1. With n = +5, the call is memmove(v, v + 5, size), the destination is below the source, so a forward copy is correct, but the ranges overlap with a distance of only five bytes.
  2. In the tested VCRuntime build, 8191 bytes uses a vector loop, while 8193 selects rep movsb. Thus 8192 is a dispatch threshold of that library build, not a hardware boundary (microsoft/STL #5506).

Measurements show that on some CPUs, including Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, and the Alder Lake P-core, forward rep movsb is exceptionally slow when source and destination differ by 1 through 63 bytes. The architectural definition guarantees the result, but not how the fast-string engine implements it. In my opinion, the measurements are consistent with a dependency-related close-overlap slow path, but that mechanism is an inference rather than a published fact, saying that the instruction necessarily copies byte-by-byte or internally uses 64-byte chunks would go beyond the evidence. Backward rep movsb (DF=1) is independently documented as suffering significant performance degradation (Intel Optimization Manual section 3.7.6.3, quoted in the earlier answer). Glibc, for example, instead branches to a backward vector path when dst > src.

Intel's optimization reference manual, volume 1 lists the favourable conditions together: forward direction, source and destination aligned to 16 bytes, a length that is a multiple of 64, and regions that do not overlap. These four are optimal-performance conditions, not a promise that missing any one always selects a byte-at-a-time path. The software developer's manual, volumes 2A to 2D specifies the repeated MOVSB result but does not specify the fast-string engine's internal width.

The reported severe case occurs on Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, and the Alder Lake P-core, but was not reproduced in the cited tests on Skylake/Coffee Lake or the Alder Lake E-core. These observations do not establish an exhaustive CPU list. FSRM was introduced with Ice Lake. Glibc uses it as a conservative indicator for applying this workaround on Intel CPUs, not as a guarantee that every FSRM implementation has the same penalty. The exact behaviour is microarchitectural.

Libraries use rep movsb because it can be fast for sufficiently large non-overlapping forward copies, with compact code and no separate tail loop (discussion and measurements). For the pre-FSRM ERMS implementations covered by the cited Intel guidance, the documented startup cost is about 35 cycles, making it unattractive for short copies. FSRM and later implementations need not have the same startup behaviour. The crossover is CPU-, alignment-, cache-, and library-dependent, and sufficiently large copies can beat some vector loops under favourable conditions, but measurements on one CPU are not guarantees for another. In this runtime-sized benchmark, the compilers call memmove. On Linux, the instruction sequence is therefore selected by the installed libc rather than by Clang versus GCC. Compilers may still inline or transform other calls when the size and alignment are known.

Yes, the library should avoid this corner case. Glibc added exactly such a check: on Intel CPUs with FSRM it avoids rep movsb when the source/destination distance modulo 4 GiB is 1 through 63 bytes and falls back to its vector path (glibc change, the check lives in memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S). According to the reported inspection in the accepted answer, MSVC's v14.50 CRT, shipped with Visual Studio 2026, added an equivalent less-than-64-byte-distance check without a CPU gate. The glibc change includes benchmark evidence that gating the workaround avoids regressions on Intel processors without FSRM. Both checks are designed to retain the ordinary rep movsb path while excluding this pathological distance case, although the cited MSVC report does not provide equivalent before-and-after benchmark data.

A caller that controls both pointers can rule the corner case out structurally instead of checking distance. FastMM4-AVX, my fork of the FastMM4 allocator originally written by Pierre le Riche, compares an already tail-adjusted count against a 2048-byte tuning threshold in its AVX-512 move routine. Because the eight-byte tail has already been removed, that comparison corresponds to a 2056-byte full block in this routine. No distance check guards its rep movsb. As far as I can tell from its intended allocator use, the routine is reached for reallocation copies after a distinct destination block has been obtained, so those particular source and destination allocations cannot overlap; establishing that property from the repository alone requires following the routine's call sites as well as inspecting the assembly.
